title: What Leaders Are Made Of
subject: English

intro: Lesson 42: Non-fiction and Act 4: good leadership and Scotland's suffering. Read the whole text, then annotate it: underline the writer's methods and note their effect in the margin.

passage.title: What Leaders Are Made Of
paras: Studies of effective leaders keep returning to a handful of qualities: honesty, fairness, self-control, courage and care for the people they serve. Notice what is missing from the list: fear. Leaders who rule through fear may be obeyed, but they are rarely trusted, and power without trust is fragile. When it cracks, it cracks all at once.

Fear works quickly. A threat can make people do what they are told by the end of the day. But it also teaches them to hide mistakes, to tell the leader only what the leader wants to hear, and to wait for the moment when the threat is gone. A leader surrounded by frightened people is a leader who no longer knows what is really happening.

Trust is slower to build. It grows when a leader keeps promises, applies the same rules to friends and rivals, admits errors and protects the weakest people in their care. Once built, it is remarkably strong: people will follow a trusted leader through hardship because they believe the hardship is shared and the purpose is good.

History offers both kinds. Some rulers held power for years through spies and punishment, only to be abandoned overnight when their armies refused to fight. Others, with far less force, were followed with loyalty that outlived them.

The lesson for any leader, from a head of state to a team captain, is the same. You can make people afraid of you, or you can make them believe in you. Only one of those will hold when the storm comes.

questions.q: What is the writer's main viewpoint?
questions.a: Good leaders are trusted, not feared; power built on fear is fragile.

questions.q: Find two methods the writer uses and explain the effect of each.
questions.a: A list of qualities; contrast between fear and trust; the metaphor of cracking; examples from history.

questions.q: How does the final paragraph end the argument?
questions.a: With a direct choice and a storm metaphor: only trust 'will hold'.

questions.q: Retrieve the five qualities and the one thing missing.
questions.a: Honesty, fairness, self-control, courage, care; missing: fear.
Personification: Scotland is a wounded body; repetition stresses its suffering under Macbeth.

questions.q: Core: in the portal response box, compare Macbeth with a good leader using the article and Act 4 scene 3. Starter: 'A good leader shows..., whereas Macbeth...'
questions.a: A comparison with two qualities, evidence from the play and the article.

questions.q: Extend: why does Malcolm test Macduff?
questions.a: Because Macbeth's deceit has made trust hard; Malcolm must be sure Macduff is not a spy.

questions.q: Stretch: how does Shakespeare use Malcolm to flatter James I?
questions.a: Malcolm models the virtuous king; James descended (it was believed) from Banquo, so good kingship is linked to him.

questions.q: According to the article, why is power based on fear fragile?
options: Without trust it can crack all at once
questions.a: C) Without trust it can crack all at once. The final sentences explain this; fear brings obedience, not trust.

questions.q: Answer the ponder in one sentence.
questions.a: A ruler holds power; a leader earns trust by serving justly.
